n: Jeremiah calls Israel to hear what the Lord says about the nations’ idols.
Don’t copy the ways of the nations or be terrified by signs in the sky, as they are. Ancient peoples feared eclipses and comets as omens; God’s people needn’t fear them.

f.w: Learn not the way of the heathen

f.g: Eclipses, comets, and other sky events read as omens by astrologers.

n: Their customs are empty: someone cuts down a tree, and a craftsman shapes it with a chisel.

f.w: the customs of the people are vain

n: They decorate it with silver and gold and nail it down so it won’t fall over. Some readers have compared this to modern Christmas trees, but the passage is about idols.
Idols are like scarecrows in a cucumber field: they can’t talk, must be carried because they can’t walk. Don’t fear them—they can’t harm you or help you.

f.g: Better: “like a scarecrow in a cucumber field.”

n: No one is like You, Lord. You are great, and Your name is mighty.

f.w: there is none like unto thee

n: Who wouldn’t fear You, King of the nations? Among all the world’s wise men and kingdoms, there is no one like You.
Idolaters are senseless and foolish; their teaching is worthless, coming from a block of wood.

f.w: the stock is a doctrine of vanities
f.g: Instruction from a piece of wood is nonsense.

n: Imported silver from Tarshish and gold from Uphaz, shaped by skilled craftsmen and dressed in royal blue and purple—it’s all just human handiwork.

f.g: A distant western port, perhaps in Spain.
An unknown gold-producing region, possibly Ophir.
Expensive dyes reserved for royalty and the wealthy.

n: But the Lord is the true God, the living God, the eternal King. The earth quakes at His anger, and nations can’t endure His wrath.
Unusually, this verse is written in Aramaic, the international language of the day—perhaps so Judah could repeat it to Babylonians: gods who didn’t make heaven and earth will vanish from the earth.

f.w: The gods that have not made the heavens and the earth
f.g: The only Aramaic verse in Jeremiah, likely a ready-made reply to foreigners.

n: God made the earth by His power, set the world in place by His wisdom, and stretched out the heavens by His understanding.

f.w: He hath made the earth by his power

n: When He speaks, the skies roar with water; He lifts clouds from the ends of the earth, sends lightning with rain, and brings wind from His storehouses. The true God controls the weather that Baal was falsely credited with.

f.w: bringeth forth the wind out of his treasures

n: Every idol maker is senseless and shamed by his idol. His image is a fraud—there’s no breath in it.

f.w: there is no breath in them

n: They are worthless, objects of mockery; when judgment comes they will perish.
But Jacob’s portion—the Lord—is nothing like them. He formed all things, and Israel is the tribe He claimed as His inheritance. His name is the Lord of Hosts.
Jeremiah turns to the coming siege: pick up your bundle and get ready to leave, you who live under siege.
God says He will sling out the land’s inhabitants like stones from a sling and press them hard so they feel it.

f.w: I will sling out the inhabitants

n: Jerusalem (or Jeremiah) cries: my wound is incurable! But I said, “This is my sickness, and I must bear it.” Accepting consequences is the first step toward healing.

f.w: Truly this is a grief, and I must bear it

n: My tent is ruined, its ropes snapped; my children are gone, and no one is left to pitch my tent again. Zion is pictured as a mother whose home and children are lost.

f.w: my children are gone forth of me

n: The shepherds (rulers) are senseless and don’t seek the Lord, so they fail and their flocks scatter. Leadership failure leads to scattering.
Listen—news is coming, a great uproar from the north, to make Judah’s towns desolate, a haunt of jackals.
A humble prayer: Lord, I know a person’s path isn’t in his own control; no one can direct his own steps. We need God’s guidance.

f.w: it is not in man that walketh to direct his steps

n: Correct me, Lord, but with fairness—not in anger, or You’d reduce me to nothing. A plea for loving discipline.
Pour out Your fury on the nations that don’t know You and don’t call on Your name, for they have devoured Jacob. Psalm 79:6-7 contains nearly the same words.

f.w: Pour out thy fury upon the heathen
